newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Maori tribe gets NZ govt apology, compensation.
newsitem.headline: Maori tribe gets NZ govt apology, compensation.

text.p: The New Zealand government on Tuesday agreed to apologise to the Whakatohea Maori tribe for the wrongful seizure of ancestral lands, and settled claims dating back to 1865.

Treaty Negotiations Minister Doug Graham and tribal representatives signed the settlement. It needs to be ratified by the eastern North Island tribe and requires legislation from the new parliament after a general election on October 12.
The tribe's claim stems from the confiscation of 70,000 hectares (175,000 acres) of land following the murder of German missionary Carl Volkner in 1865.

One of the three men hanged in 1866 for his murder, Chief Mokomoko, was pardoned 126 years later by then Governor General Dame Catherine Tizard because he had been convicted after a one-day hearing and on flimsy and contradictory evidence.

Under the deal, the tribe will become owners of the Opotiki police station, courthouse and four police properties which it will lease back to the government. Financial settlement is for NZ$40 million (US$28 million).
Spokesman John Delamere said the Whakatohea (pronounced fokatoa) would have preferred the return of all its land, but it had to be realistic and knew the government owned little land in the region.
"Some of our people will be concerned, but we will be recommending they accept the settlement because it's the best we can do, given the parameters," he said.
Recognition of the unfairness of the confiscation had been admitted since 1908 when a government commission found the tribe had "very little land left in their hands".
In 1921, the Native Land Commission said the penalty had been unduly harsh, and had been influenced by public outrage about the missionary's murder.
It found the land confiscation excessive, illegal and inappropriate as it punished the innocent and guilty alike.
The settlement calls for the government to apologise for the confiscation while Whakatohea will acknowledge the settlement as "fair, final and durable."

The conservative National Party government has been keen to make progress on Maori claims to win Maori and liberal voters, while the tribes are keen to grasp the opportunity of the government's willingness to end years of grievances.
Last year the government paid NZ$170 million and returned 15,790 hectares (39,000 acres) of land to the North Island Tainui tribe.

In June, the government accepted a tribunal's finding that virtually the entire west coast of the North Island province of Taranaki had been illegally confiscated. Details of that settlement have not been agreed.
The Ngai Tahu (pronouned nai ta-hu), the main South Island tribe, said last month it was on the verge of an agreement with the government and may settle before the election.
The government has set aside NZ$1 billion to settle claims, though many Maori argue that the sum is arbitrary, insufficient and was fixed without consulting them.
